NOVELTY STATEMENT
Standard practice delivers a MONITORING/INDICATION scheme via acoustic emission sensors or continuous seal-pressure transducers installed on the plunger to detect leak initiation. My same-class mechanism departs by inferring the seal clearance change through the thermodynamic efficiency drop in the existing discharge pressure pulsation spectrum and motor current harmonic distortion, without adding any physical probe. The failure-physics connection is that as the plunger seal wears, high-pressure discharge fluid recirculates into the suction side during the compression stroke, reducing the effective volumetric work done by the motor and altering the pressure pulse rise-time and peak amplitude relative to speed.

PHYSICS CHECK
Governing relation: The discharge pressure pulse $P(t)$ is proportional to the trapped volume $V(t)$ and the polytropic work term. Seal leak adds a backflow path $Q_{leak}(t)$, reducing net discharge flow. Motor current $I(t)$ represents total power input; efficiency $\eta = \frac{P_{hyd}}{P_{elec}}$ drops as seal clearance $d$ increases because parasitic recirculation power $P_{leak} \propto d^3$. Magnitude verification: A 10% increase in seal clearance typically causes a 1-2% drop in pump efficiency and a measurable shift in the fundamental pressure pulse frequency component amplitude due to the changed head loss curve; this shift is detectable in standard FFT of recorded pressure data with <0.5% SNR.
